title: Science and faith
hook: physicist-priest John Polkinghorne saw science and faith as two windows

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Mbiti and African theology: a person as a thread in a cloth. Your line was I am because we are. Who did you thank out loud? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

Why is the kettle boiling? One answer: the burner heats the water, the molecules speed up, and at the right temperature the water turns to steam. Another answer: because I'd like a cup of tea. Both answers are true. Neither one cancels the other. And you'd look a little strange if you insisted that only one of them was allowed. That small kitchen puzzle is one John Polkinghorne used. He was a physicist who worked on the tiniest pieces of matter, the particles inside the atom. Then he left his professorship, trained for the ministry, and became an Anglican priest. Today's word is the two things he refused to choose between.

Polkinghorne didn't think science and faith were fighting over the same ground. Picture them as two windows in one house, looking out at the same world. His own phrase was binocular vision: two eyes, set a little apart, give you depth that one eye can't. First window: science. It asks how. How do stars form? How does the kettle boil? It tests, measures, and changes its mind when the evidence says so. He left research physics, but after he was ordained he kept writing about science for the rest of his life. Second window: faith. It asks why, and what for. Is there purpose? Is there love behind the light? The Psalms look up at the same sky a physicist studies and see something more: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Third, the place where the windows meet. Polkinghorne was struck that the universe can be understood at all. Mathematics, worked out on paper, turns out to fit the way the world actually behaves. Why should that be? For him, that was a clue: a world that makes sense, as if made by a mind. He offered it as a hint worth following, not as a proof. Fourth, the humility of both. Science says, we don't know yet, let's look. Faith, at its best, says something similar. The psalmist, gazing at the night sky, asks: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" That's not an answer. It's wonder. Polkinghorne thought a scientist and a believer could share that same wonder, and that one person could be both.

Here's the practice: look at the world through both windows. Choose one thing you can see right now: a plant, your hand, the light through a window, a cup. Settle, and breathe. First, look through the how window. What is it made of? How does it work? What would a scientist say about it? Then, slowly, look through the why window. What is it for? What does it mean to you? Is there anything in it worth thanking someone for? If you pray, you can offer that thanks to God. If you don't, just let both views sit side by side. The bell holds the time.
Science and faith. For John Polkinghorne, two windows on one world: one asks how, the other asks why, and together they give depth.

Your line: two windows. Today, when you hear a how answer, a weather report, a news story, a diagnosis, ask the why question too, and when you hear a why, ask the how. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Some Christians work as scientists and see no conflict between the two; churches differ on how they relate scripture and science, and some hold study groups on the question.

notes: Polkinghorne paraphrased throughout. Confirm: the kettle example (how vs why); 'binocular vision' as his image; the intelligibility of the universe and the fit of mathematics as a clue, not a proof.
'Two windows' is the outline's image; the script presents it as his way of seeing alongside his own 'binocular vision'. Confirm this is fair to him.
Biography: particle physicist, left his professorship (Cambridge) to train for the Anglican priesthood; no dates or ages given by design. Confirm 'in the middle of a successful career'.
